name: Human nature

source.title: Philosophy and the Science of Human Nature (PHIL 181)

draftedBy: Claude, from Yale's lectures and transcripts, for Bryan to keep, change or strike
why: Old questions about how to live, tested against what science now knows about people. Why we cheat when no one is looking, why we snooze the alarm, what makes a life go well, what we owe each other. Yale's course, lecture by lecture, with our everyday pictures and quizzes added.
outcomes: Tell apart looking fair and being fair, in yourself first.
Set things up ahead of time so the choice you want still wins when temptation is close.

units.title: The Ring of Gyges: being fair or seeming fair
units.outcome: Tell apart looking fair and being fair, in yourself first.
units.needIt: When no one checks (the self-checkout, the tax form, the unwatched tip jar) you find out what you really value. Knowing that your own mind will call a bent rule "fair" lets you catch it, and spot it in others.
units.why: Plato's brother Glaucon asked: if a ring made you invisible, would you still be good? A psychologist named Daniel Batson then tested it. Given a coin to decide fairly, most people kept the good task for themselves anyway, and still rated themselves as moral.
units.reachesYou: Splitting a bill, dividing chores, grading your own work, the expense report, the "random" pick that keeps landing on you, the leader who sets the rules and keeps winning.
units.do: This week, the next time you settle something with a coin, a draw or a rule, decide before it lands that you will keep the result. Notice the pull to flip again.

quiz.q: In Glaucon's story, what does the Ring of Gyges let you do?
choices: Turn invisible, so no one sees what you do
quiz.why: The ring separates what you do from how you look. That is the whole test: how would you act if your reputation could not be hurt?
quiz.quote: If your act of immorality were invisible to the world, if you could behave immorally and nobody would see you, so that your reputation remained unscathed, how is it that you would behave?

quiz.q: Glaucon claims people act fairly mainly because...
quiz.why: Glaucon argues that fairness is like medicine: you take it for what it gets you, here a good name.
quiz.quote: That the only reason people act and conform with the laws of morality is because they will gain good reputations thereby.

quiz.q: In Batson's study, people flipped a coin to decide who got the fun task. How many of them gave it to themselves?
choices: About half, as a fair coin would
quiz.why: A fair coin gives you the fun task half the time. Nine in ten means most people found a way around the coin, then kept the result.
quiz.quote: What happens is that upon flipping the coin, 90% of them assign themselves to the positive condition!

quiz.q: How did those coin flippers rate their own fairness?
quiz.why: This is the hypocrisy part: the coin let them feel fair while doing the selfish thing.
quiz.quote: rate themselves as having acted in an extraordinarily moral way: seven on a scale of nine

quiz.q: What made people actually follow the coin?
quiz.why: Feeling watched, even by your own reflection, brings behavior back to fair. The same lecture tells of eyes taped over an honor-system coffee jar raising payments.
quiz.quote: And if they are facing the mirror and flipping the coin, they behave 50%: exactly as chance would predict.

scene.analogy: Flipping for the last slice of pizza, until you win
map: bending the rule when no one checks

beats.say: You still feel fair. You flipped a coin.
In the lab, 9 in 10 kept the good task.
Add a mirror, and the cheating stops.

partials: Glaucon asked: if a ring made you invisible, would you still be good?
Given a coin to split the tasks fairly, most of Batson's subjects kept the good task anyway.
The same people still rated themselves as moral.
Facing a mirror and flipping the coin, people split the tasks exactly as chance would.
"Best two out of three," said only after losing the flip.
crystal.key: People want to seem fair more than to be fair, and being watched, even by yourself, closes the gap.

decoys.text: People are just selfish, and nothing changes that.
decoys.why: With a mirror facing them, people split the tasks as fairly as chance. Something small changed it.

decoys.text: Using a fair process makes the result fair.
decoys.why: Batson's subjects had a coin and still kept the good task. A process only works if you keep its result.

crystal.aha: Every partial is the gap between looking fair and being fair, and what happens when someone, even you, is watching.

units.title: Weakness of the will: why the snooze button wins
units.outcome: Set things up ahead of time so the choice you want still wins when temptation is close.
units.needIt: Every "I'll start tomorrow" runs on this. Knowing why the snooze button wins at 5:30 lets you arrange things the night before, so the better choice wins in the morning: money, food, work, sleep, habits.
units.why: Asked a month ahead, almost everyone waits two extra days for $6 over $5. Asked today, one in five grabs the $5. Up close, a small reward looks bigger than it is. Aristotle named the problem; Ainslie measured it; Mischel's marshmallow children show what beats it.
units.reachesYou: The snooze button, the cupcake on the diet, the impulse buy, the paper left to the last night, the savings plan that starts next month, the phone you check "for a second".
units.do: Pick one temptation you lose to. Before it comes, do one "mast" move: put the alarm across the room, the phone in another room, the snacks out of the house, or make it a rule ("no screens after 10") so you do not decide case by case.

quiz.q: Offered $5 today or $6 in two days, some students took the $5. Offered the same choice a month out, what did they do?
quiz.why: Same two days, same extra dollar. Only the distance changed. Up close, the sooner reward looms larger.
quiz.quote: 20% of you were preferring to take $5 today over $6 on Thursday, even though almost none of you wanted to take the same decision in a month.

quiz.q: What did the psychologist George Ainslie call this pattern?
quiz.why: The value we feel for a reward drops steeply with delay, then jumps as the reward gets close.

quiz.q: Mischel's children waited longest for the second marshmallow when they...
choices: Thought about how tasty it was
Pretended it was a picture, or thought about it in the abstract
quiz.why: Keeping the treat vivid in mind made it hard to resist. Cooling it down (imaginary, abstract) let four-year-olds wait about 18 minutes.
quiz.quote: So the presence of the temptation before your mind is part of what makes the temptation difficult to resist.

quiz.q: Odysseus had himself tied to the mast so he could hear the Sirens and not steer to them. Which everyday move is the same idea?
choices: Putting your alarm clock across the room
Waiting to decide in the morning
quiz.why: Decide while you are clear-headed, then make it hard to act on the temptation later.
quiz.quote: You can put your alarm clock all the way across the room you can take the cupcakes out of your house, you can put your credit card in a glass of water in the freezer.

quiz.q: How does a rule like "no dessert after 4 pm" help?
choices: You stop deciding case by case
quiz.why: A rule makes one cupcake stand for all cupcakes, so "just this once" stops being a fresh decision every time.
quiz.quote: if I have a principle that I don't eat dessert after 4:00 pm, then it's easy. I don't have to make a decision on a case-by-case basis.

scene.analogy: The 5:30 alarm you set the night before

beats.say: Night: "I'll get up at 5:30 and write."
Up close, the small reward looks bigger.

plan.label: The larger, later reward
plan.sub: what you chose with a clear head

beats.say: Tie yourself to the mast: alarm across the room.

partials: Asked a month ahead, almost everyone waits two extra days for $6 over $5.
Asked today, one in five grabs the $5.
Odysseus had himself tied to the mast before he sailed past the sirens.
Mischel's children sat in front of one marshmallow now, or two if they waited.
The alarm clock set across the room the night before.
crystal.key: A small reward up close looks bigger than it is, so decide ahead of time and set things up so the choice you want still wins.

decoys.text: Weak will is a flaw of character: you have it or you do not.
decoys.why: The same people chose $6 a month ahead and $5 today. The distance changed the choice, not the person.

decoys.text: Just try harder in the moment.
decoys.why: The moment is when the small reward looks biggest. Odysseus did not trust himself at the sirens; he planned before.

crystal.aha: Every partial is the same curve: far away you choose well, up close the small thing looms, and only a move made in advance holds.

gendler.name: Tamar Gendler
gendler.did: Taught this course at Yale in 2011 and gave it away free through Open Yale Courses, pairing old philosophy with new psychology.

plato.name: Plato
plato.did: Wrote the Republic about 375 BC, where his brother Glaucon tells the story of the ring that makes you invisible.

batson.name: C. Daniel Batson
batson.did: Ran the coin-flip studies on moral hypocrisy: most people kept the good task while rating themselves fair, unless they faced a mirror.

aristotle.name: Aristotle
aristotle.did: Plato's student. In the Ethics, Book VII, he named weakness of will: knowing the better thing and doing the other.

ainslie.name: George Ainslie
ainslie.did: Measured how people and animals undervalue later rewards in a steep curve, so the sooner, smaller one wins up close.

mischel.name: Walter Mischel
mischel.did: Ran the marshmallow studies and found that how children thought about the treat changed how long they could wait.

nozick.name: Robert Nozick
nozick.did: Argued that principles bind us like Odysseus's ropes: one act stands for the whole class, so we stop deciding case by case.
